---
title: "Design Philosophy & When NOT to Use This"
---

captain-hook treats a hook as typed, declarative data you can test inline and check with a type
checker, not a shell snippet you hand-write in `settings.json`.

## A hook is data, not a script

A native Claude Code hook is a command string in `settings.json`. Claude Code pipes the event to
that command's stdin and reads a verdict from its stdout. The matcher, the event filter, and the
verdict all live as text inside a JSON file. Nothing reads that text until Claude Code fires the
event, so a typo, a wrong field name, or a broken regex stays invisible until the moment it
should have fired.

captain-hook moves the same description into Python objects. You register a hook by calling a
typed function:

```python
from captain_hook import block_command

block_command(
    ["git", "stash"],
    reason="Use jj instead of git stash",
)
```

The event target, the conditions, and the verdict are now values with types. The
[primitives reference](../reference/primitives.qmd) lists every builder and the verdict each one
produces; the [conditions reference](../reference/conditions.qmd) lists every filter; the
[events reference](../reference/events.qmd) lists every lifecycle moment you can target.

### You can test a hook before it ships

Each primitive carries inline `tests`, mapping a sample event to the verdict you expect.

```python
from captain_hook import block_command, Input, Block, Allow

block_command(
    ["git", "stash"],
    reason="Use jj instead of git stash",
    tests={
        Input(command="git stash"): Block(pattern="jj"),
        Input(command="git status"): Allow(),
    },
)
```

`uvx capt-hook test` runs every inline case and exits non-zero on the first failure, so a broken
matcher fails in your terminal or in CI instead of in a live session. A shell hook in
`settings.json` has nowhere to put this. You discover a regex mistake when the hook either blocks
the wrong command or stays silent on the right one, mid-conversation, with no record of why.

### The type checker reads your hook

The arguments to `block_command`, `hook`, and the condition builders are typed. Pass a condition
where an event flag belongs, or misname a verdict field, and pyright flags it before the hook
ever runs. A regex inside a JSON string is opaque to every tool you own. A condition object is a
value the type checker, your editor, and the test runner all read.

### The wiring is mechanical

You do not hand-edit the matcher block in `settings.json`. captain-hook reads your hook
definitions and generates the wiring for you, so the `settings.json` entry and the hook it points
at cannot drift apart. The JSON becomes generated output, not a file you maintain by hand. One
description of the hook lives in your Python; the JSON follows from it.

## What you give up by hand-writing shell hooks

A `settings.json` hook is a string. It is invisible to the type checker, untestable without a
live session, and wired by hand, so the matcher and the script it invokes drift apart over time.
You read the regex, guess what it matches, and find out when it fires. As a directory of these
grows, the cost of each compounds, because none of them composes, none carries a test, and none
fails loudly when it breaks.

captain-hook spends a dependency and a Python file to buy back that visibility. The hook becomes
a value you can read, test, type-check, and compose. For a directory you maintain over months,
that is the trade worth making.

## When plain settings.json hooks suffice

The trade is not always worth it. Reach for a native `settings.json` hook, and skip captain-hook,
when:

- The hook is a one-liner you will not change. A single `echo` on `Notification`, or a formatter
  that always runs after every edit, has nothing to test and nothing to type-check. A JSON string
  is the lighter tool.
- The logic already lives in a script you trust. If you run an existing linter or a vetted shell
  script, wrapping it in a Python hook adds a layer without adding a check.
- You cannot take the dependency. captain-hook runs through `uvx`, which needs
  [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) on the machine. An environment without uv, or one that forbids
  fetching a tool at runtime, rules it out. A native hook needs only the shell.
- You are wiring a handful of hooks, once. The payoff comes from testability and mechanical wiring
  across many hooks over time. For two or three hooks you will never touch again, the JSON is
  enough.

captain-hook earns its place when a hook directory grows, changes, and needs to stay correct
across edits. When the hook is small, static, and trusted, the native mechanism is the right
amount of machinery. Choose by how much the hook will change and how badly a silent break would
cost you.
